question: What cycles of nature and of history does the Teacher observe in verses 4 to 11?
The Teacher presents himself as a wise king who investigated everything: why does he conclude that “with much wisdom comes much sorrow”?
The word הֶבֶל (hevel, “vapor, breath, futility”) opens the book in verse 2 and returns in verse 14: what does this image of vapor suggest about life “under the sun”?
“The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing”: in what area do you notice this continual dissatisfaction?
What projects and pleasures does the Teacher pursue in verses 4 to 10, and what does he say he gained from all of it?
After so much disillusionment, the Teacher says that eating, drinking and finding satisfaction in work is “from the hand of God”: how does this conclusion relate to the rest of the chapter?
The word שִׂמְחָה (simchah, “joy, pleasure”) appears in verses 1, 2, 10 and 26: how does the Teacher's view of joy change over the course of the chapter?
The Teacher is distressed at leaving the fruit of his labor to whoever comes after him: how do you deal with the idea that you will not control the fate of what you have built?
What pairs of opposites does the poem of verses 1 to 8 present, and is there any order or grouping among them?
What might it mean that God “has set eternity in the hearts” of men, yet no one can fathom His work from beginning to end?
The word עֵת (‘et, “time, appointed season”) is repeated throughout the poem and returns in verse 17: what difference is there between this “right time” and the mere passing of hours?
There is “a time to be silent and a time to speak”: in what present situation do you need to discern which of the two is yours?
What does the Teacher see when he looks at the oppression under the sun, and what does he repeat twice about the oppressed?
The Teacher criticizes both work driven by envy and the endless work of someone who labors alone: what balance does verse 6 propose between these extremes?
The word שְׁנַיִם (shenayim, “two”) appears in verses 9, 11 and 12: what concrete advantages of companionship does the Teacher list?
“If one falls down, his companion can lift him up”: who lifts you up when you fall, and whom have you been lifting up?
What advice does the Teacher give about behavior in the house of God, about words and about vows?
Why does whoever loves money “never have enough money,” and what does the laborer's sleep have to do with this?
The verb נָדַר (nadar, “make a vow”) is repeated in verses 4 and 5: why does the Teacher think it better not to promise than to promise and not fulfill?
“God is in heaven and you are on earth, so let your words be few”: what would your prayer be like with fewer words and more listening?
What situation of someone who has everything and cannot enjoy it does the Teacher describe in verses 1 to 6?
The chapter ends with two questions: who knows what is good, and who can tell what will come after: what do these unanswered questions reveal about human limits?
The word נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh, “soul, appetite, desire”) appears in verses 7 and 9: what does the Teacher say about the appetite that is never satisfied?
“Better what the eye can see than the wandering of desire”: what do you already have before your eyes that you have not been enjoying?
How many “better is...” comparisons appear in verses 1 to 8, and what do they value that is usually avoided?
The Teacher says “do not be overly righteous, and do not make yourself too wise”: what excess of righteousness or wisdom does he seem to be criticizing?
The word אֵבֶל (evel, “mourning”) appears in verses 2 and 4: why would the house of mourning teach more than the house of feasting?
“Do not say, ‘Why were the old days better than these?’”: in what area have you been living on nostalgia instead of living in the present?
What advice does the Teacher give about the relationship with the king and his word in verses 2 to 5?
The Teacher notes that delay of judgment encourages evil and at the same time affirms that it will go well with those who fear God: how does he hold these two observations together?
The word עֵת (‘et, “time”) appears in verses 5, 6 and 9: what does the wise heart know about time, and what does the human being not know?
The Teacher admits that not even the wise man can comprehend the work of God: how do you live with what you cannot understand?
What five examples does verse 11 give that “the race is not to the swift,” and what happens to all of them?
“A live dog is better than a dead lion”: what value does the Teacher give to present life, and how does this connect with the view of death he expresses here?
The word מִסְכֵּן (misken, “poor”) appears in verses 15 and 16: what does the story of the poor wise man who saved the city teach about wisdom and recognition?
“Go, eat your bread with joy”: what keeps you from enjoying with gratitude the simple things God gives?
What risks of everyday work appear in verses 8 to 11, and what place does wisdom have in verse 10?
The Teacher sees slaves on horseback and princes on foot: what social disorder is he denouncing, and why does he call it an “error” of those in authority?
The word יִתְרוֹן (yitron, “advantage, profit”) appears in verses 10 and 11: in what situations does wisdom bring advantage, and when does the advantage come too late?
“A little folly outweighs wisdom and honor,” like dead flies in perfume: what small attitude may be spoiling something good in your life?
What images of the field and of nature does the Teacher use in verses 1 to 6, and what do they advise about acting in the face of uncertainty?
The Teacher invites the young man to rejoice and, in the same verse, recalls God's judgment: how do joy and responsibility combine here?
The verb זָרַע (zara‘, “sow”) appears in verses 4 and 6: why does someone who waits for perfect conditions never sow?
“Cast your bread upon the waters”: where could you be generous with no guarantee of return?
What images do verses 2 to 7 use (many read them as a portrait of old age), and what happens to the dust and the spirit in verse 7?
After repeating “everything is futile,” the book concludes with “fear God and keep His commandments”: does this conclusion resolve or leave open the tensions of the book?
The word קֹהֶלֶת (qohelet, “Teacher, the one who gathers”) appears in verses 8, 9 and 10: what does the epilogue say about this figure's work?
“Remember your Creator in the days of your youth”: what would it mean for you to remember the Creator at the stage of life you are in?
